title: ‘Babylon on the Potomac’: Pete Hegseth’s Radical DC Church Attracts Government Elites
gist: WIRED identified around a dozen Trump administration officials—including senior Pentagon, Navy, DHS, HHS, DOJ and DFC figures—who have attended Christ Church DC, a Capitol Hill outpost of Doug Wilson's CREC network that arrived after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's confirmation. The piece frames the church as a deliberate channel for Wilson's theocratic, Christian nationalist agenda to gain influence inside the federal government, with Hegseth as the key enabler.

themes.theme: Christ Church DC as an influence node

insights.claim: Christ Church DC, part of Doug Wilson's Moscow, Idaho-based CREC network, opened on Capitol Hill roughly a year ago after Pete Hegseth was confirmed as defense secretary, and WIRED identified around a dozen government officials who have attended it.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Maps an informal network linking a fringe religious movement to defense, intelligence and finance decision-makers.
insights.locator: WIRED has identified around a dozen government

insights.claim: Wilson is raising funds to buy a permanent building near Capitol Hill for Christ Church DC, signaling a long-term commitment to influencing Washington.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Indicates this influence effort is structural and likely to persist rather than a transient phenomenon.
insights.quote: We are here for the long haul
insights.locator: Wilson calls DC “Babylon on the Potomac,”

insights.claim: Researcher Peter Bell argues Wilson's expansion into DC would not have been possible without Hegseth, and that a church at the foot of the Capitol is Wilson's clearest route to getting only Christians into office.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Ties the movement's policy reach to Hegseth's tenure, making it sensitive to personnel changes at the Pentagon.

insights.claim: Wilson's long-term strategy, per Bell, is bottom-up: put Christians in office, legislate Christian morality, and let Christian culture emerge among the populace over time.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Frames a gradual institutional strategy whose policy effects would compound across social and regulatory domains.
insights.quote: Put Christians in office, legislate Christian morality, let that simmer among the populace, and Christian culture eventually emerges.

insights.claim: Doug Wilson's stated goal is to turn America into a theocracy governed by biblical law, with public executions, non-Christians barred from office, and women submitting to husbands rather than voting; he advocated repealing the 19th Amendment as recently as 2024.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Highlights the policy extremity of a movement now proximate to senior officials, a source of political and social risk.
insights.locator: The church is part of Pastor Doug Wilson’s

insights.claim: Wilson spreads his influence through a network of around 160 churches and hundreds of CREC-accredited schools and colleges across the US and internationally.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Shows organizational scale beyond Idaho, relevant to gauging the durability of the movement's influence.

insights.claim: As defense secretary, Hegseth introduced a monthly Pentagon prayer service, created an office of religious affairs, invoked scripture about the war in Iran, and invited Wilson to speak at Pentagon prayer sessions twice this year.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Religious framing of military policy, including the Iran war, can shape defense decision-making and escalation rhetoric.
insights.quote: while we wage physical war, we all know the real battle is spiritual
insights.locator: As secretary, Hegseth has invoked scripture

insights.claim: Church attendees include Justin Overbaugh, deputy undersecretary of war for intelligence and security, and Nate Halverson, a New Saint Andrews College graduate with no military background appointed chief of staff to the Navy's assistant secretary for manpower and reserve affairs.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Ideologically aligned appointees without traditional credentials in sensitive intelligence and personnel roles may affect defense institutional quality.
insights.locator: Wilson’s reach into the US government now

insights.claim: Mikey Weinstein of the Military Religious Freedom Foundation estimates about half of Christian active-duty service members (who were 70 percent of the force in 2019) adhere to Christian nationalist ideology, often emulating their leaders.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Suggests ideological shifts within the military that could affect cohesion, recruitment and civil-military relations.

insights.claim: Attendees outside the Pentagon include DHS intelligence undersecretary Matthew Kozma, HHS global affairs director Bethany Kozma (both Project 2025 contributors), DOJ lawyers, and Stephen Duggan, CFO of the US International Development Finance Corporation.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Ideological alignment at the DFC and DHS could influence overseas investment and security priorities.
insights.locator: Trump administration couple Bethany and Matthew Kozma

insights.claim: Project 2025 included a plan to infuse Christian nationalist ideology into all levels of US government, and Trump signed an executive order creating a task force to investigate 'anti-Christian bias' in government departments.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Indicates policy machinery that can steer hiring, grants and regulation along ideological lines.
